title: Verbs, and why they always come last
goal: Form polite-style (해요체) verbs from the dictionary form, use the object particle 을/를, and describe daily activities in full sentences.
bekal: turn the dictionary form -다 into the polite form -아요/어요
build sentences in subject – object – verb order
name the ten most common daily activities
combine time, place and activity in one sentence

dialogs.title: 대화 — Chatting at a café
dialogs.intro: Ani and Suji are meeting for the first time. Notice that in every sentence the verb lands in last place — the meaning isn't complete until the very last word.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: What do you do every day, Ani?
lines.literal: Ani — Ms. — as-for — every-day — what — do?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: In the morning I study Korean. Then in the afternoon I work.
lines.literal: morning-at — Korean-language — object — study. and — afternoon-at — work.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: At a café. I make coffee.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Is it fun? Isn't it hard?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: It's a bit hard. But I meet lots of people.
lines.literal: a-little — hard. but — people — object — a-lot — meet.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: That's nice. What do you do in the evening?
lines.literal: good — huh. evening-at — as-for — what — do?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Usually I watch dramas at home. Then I listen to music.
lines.literal: usually — home-at — drama — object — watch. and — music — object — listen.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Yes! I learn Korean through dramas.
lines.literal: yes! drama — with — Korean-language — object — learn.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: No wonder your Korean is so good.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Oh no, I still have a long way to go.

notes: **The verb always comes last, no exceptions.** Korean word order is **subject – adverbials – object – verb**. 저는 카페에서 커피를 만들어요 = "I at-café coffee make". That's why Koreans can listen to the very end before knowing what you mean, and why you mustn't stop mid-sentence.

**Because particles mark each role, everything except the verb can be reshuffled.** 커피를 카페에서 만들어요 is still correct and means the same. Only one thing can't move: the verb stays at the end. English doesn't have this freedom.

**아니에요 is used to deflect compliments.** When praised, the standard Korean response is to deny it — 아니에요 or 아직 멀었어요 ("still far off"). Accepting with 감사합니다 isn't wrong, but deflecting first sounds much more natural.

**한국어 and 한국말 both mean "Korean language".** 한국어 is more neutral and used for the language as a subject; 한국말 is more colloquial and stresses the spoken language. Note that 한국말 is read *hangungmal* — ㄱ becomes ㅇ before ㅁ.
**많이 (a lot) goes right before the verb**, not after the object as in English. 사람을 **많이** 만나요, not 많이 사람을 만나요. Korean adverbs almost always stick to the verb they describe.
**들어요 (listen) comes from 듣다, not 들다.** It's an irregular ㄷ verb: ㄷ turns into ㄹ before a vowel. 듣다 → 들어요. Several important verbs follow this pattern; the list is in the summary pages at the back.
**보통 (usually) and 매일 (every day)** are two adverbs that instantly make your story sound natural. Without them, sentences about daily routines sound like a report of a one-off event.
**그래서 means "so, therefore", 그리고 means "and then".** These two connectors start a sentence and turn a choppy story into a flowing one. The third of the set is 하지만 ("but").

grammars.title: Forming 해요체 from the dictionary form
body: Every Korean verb ends in **다** in its dictionary form. Remove 다, and what's left is the **stem**. Every other form — present, past, want, can — is built on that stem.
For the everyday polite form, look at the **last vowel in the stem**.
after: **If the stem ends in a vowel, it merges with the ending** so that two vowels don't collide:
가다 → 가**아**요 → **가요** (ㅏ + ㅏ merge into one). 만나다 → **만나요**. 보다 → **봐요** (ㅗ + ㅏ become ㅘ). 마시다 → **마셔요** (ㅣ + ㅓ become ㅕ). 배우다 → **배워요** (ㅜ + ㅓ become ㅝ). 주다 → **줘요**.
⚠️ This merging isn't decoration — unmerged forms (가아요, 보아요) sound like a 1970s textbook. Always merge.

**하다 is the most productive verb in Korean.** Hundreds of nouns become verbs just by adding it: 공부 (study) → 공부하다, 일 (work) → 일하다, 사랑 (love) → 사랑하다, 요리 (cooking) → 요리하다, 운동 (exercise) → 운동하다. All of them become -해요.

grammars.title: The object particle 을/를
body: Marks the thing that **receives** the action. Its form depends on the last letter of the noun, like almost every Korean particle.
after: **In fast speech 을/를 is often dropped** — 밥 먹어요 sounds perfectly natural. But don't copy that until the full form is automatic: in writing and exams it's required, and long sentences get blurry without it.

⚠️ Some Korean verbs take an object where English uses a preposition, and vice versa. 친구**를** 만나요 = "meet a friend" (not 친구에게). 버스**를** 타요 = "ride/get on the bus". Learn the pairs; don't translate them.

blocks.text: These twenty verbs cover most A1 conversation. Learn them **in pairs** — dictionary form and 해요 form together — because you'll need both.
A complete Korean sentence is stacked like building blocks, from the outermost to the innermost. The standard order: **who – when – where – what – does what**.
Practice by swapping one column at a time, not the whole sentence at once. The ability to build long sentences comes from swapping parts, not from memorizing whole sentences.

exercises.prompt: Change these dictionary forms into 해요체.
Translate into Korean. Watch the word order.
items: In the morning I drink coffee.
I watch Korean dramas every day.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
